t: Number of Ways to Rearrange Sticks With K Sticks Visible — A Stirling-Numbers Counting DP
o:
**Understanding the problem**

Sticks of lengths 1..n must be lined up so that exactly k of them are visible from the left, where a stick is visible when nothing taller stands before it. Visibility is therefore decided by prefix maxima: walking left to right, a position sets a new maximum exactly when its stick is visible.

**Walking through Example 1:** n = 3, k = 2 gives the arrangements [1,3,2], [2,3,1], [2,1,3] — three ways. Note [1,2,3] would show all three sticks and [3,...] shows only stick 3, so k pins down the structure tightly.

**Example 2:** n = 5, k = 5 forces strictly increasing order [1,2,3,4,5], the single arrangement where every element is a new prefix maximum.

**What the constraints imply:** n and k reach 1000, so an O(n*k) dynamic program (~10^6 states) is the intended scale; the raw answer is astronomically large (it equals a Stirling number of the first kind), hence the modulus.
k: A stick is visible exactly when it is a strict prefix maximum, so visibility is fully determined by relative order, not by absolute positions.
Condition on the shortest stick, length 1: placed first it is always visible; anywhere else it is invisible and can be removed without changing anyone else's visibility.

Removing that invisible shortest stick leaves an arrangement of n-1 sticks with k visible, and reinserting it into any of n-1 non-first slots reconstructs the original — giving the recurrence f(n,k) = f(n-1,k-1) + (n-1)*f(n-1,k), i.e., unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind.

a.i: Define f(i, j) as the number of arrangements of sticks 1..i showing exactly j sticks from the left. Split on where the shortest stick sits: first position means it is visible and the rest is any f(i-1, j-1) arrangement of the taller sticks; any other position means it hides, it can be deleted to yield an f(i-1, j) arrangement, and there are i-1 slots to put it back into. Memoizing the (i, j) states makes each state cost O(1).
s: Base cases: f(0, 0) = 1, and f(i, 0) = 0 for i >= 1 (some stick is always visible).
Recurrence: f(i, j) = f(i-1, j-1) + (i-1) * f(i-1, j), taken modulo 10^9 + 7.
Memoize every computed state in a table indexed by (i, j).
a.t: O(n*k) — each of the nk states is computed once with O(1) work; about 10^6 operations at n = k = 1000.
a.sp: O(n*k) — the memoization table plus O(n) recursion stack.

a.n: Approach 2: Bottom-Up Tabulation with Rolling Rows
a.i: The same recurrence fills naturally from small i upward, and row i reads only row i-1, so two rows suffice instead of the full table. Iterating also sidesteps recursion-depth limits. Row i only needs entries up to j = min(i, k) because i sticks can show at most i records.
s: Initialize dp[0] = 1 (the empty arrangement sees nothing) and dp[j] = 0 otherwise.
For i = 1..n rebuild ndp: ndp[j] = dp[j-1] + (i-1) * dp[j] for j = 1..min(i, k), modulo 10^9 + 7.
Swap ndp into dp after each round.
a.t: O(n*k) — the double loop performs about sum over i of min(i,k) <= n*k modular updates.
a.sp: O(k) — only the previous and current rows are kept.

w: Derive the recurrence aloud using the shortest-stick argument, then code the rolling-row version — it is short and immune to stack limits. Sanity checks before submitting: n = k forces the strictly increasing permutation (answer 1), k = 1 gives (n-1)! mod p (only stick n anchors visibility while everything else hides behind it), and Example 1 reproduces 3 through rows [1,0,0] -> [0,1,0] -> [0,1,1] -> [0,2,3]. Pitfalls: multiplying by i instead of i-1, letting the product (i-1) * dp[j] overflow before reducing in C++/Java, and Python recursion-limit crashes in Approach 1 without setrecursionlimit. Follow-ups worth mentioning: counting arrangements visible from both sides simultaneously (combine two Stirling tables with inclusion-exclusion), or computing the entire visibility distribution f(n, .) in one pass — which this DP already does.
